analysis.one_liner: Limits presidential power, bans self-pardons, and enforces ethics rules against officials' self-enrichment.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: it sat in the Homeland Security Committee from September 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put binding limits on the presidency and other federal officeholders: it bans a president from pardoning himself, makes it a crime to bribe officials with pardons, bans the president and other officials from accepting gifts or payments from foreign or state governments, and lets Congress sue to force them to give back such payments. It would also require presidents and vice presidents to publish 10 years of tax returns, speed up court enforcement of congressional subpoenas, require Congress to approve national emergency declarations within 20 days, strengthen whistleblower protections, require cause to fire inspectors general, and require campaigns to report foreign contacts. The Senate introduced it on September 30, 2021, sent it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and no vote ever happened before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want a presidency bound by enforceable rules rather than norms: they gain checks on self-pardons, self-enrichment, secret legal opinions, unilateral emergencies, and obstruction of congressional oversight. Federal whistleblowers and inspectors general also gain stronger protections.

how_it_helps.text: Void any presidential self-pardon and make offering or accepting a pardon in exchange for anything of value an explicit bribery offense [S3].

Ban the president and other officials from accepting emoluments from foreign or state governments, including through their private businesses, and authorize Congress to sue to force disgorgement of the value [S3].
Require presidential and vice presidential candidates to file their 10 most recent income tax returns with the Federal Election Commission [S2].

Require every national emergency the president declares to expire within 20 days unless Congress passes a joint resolution of approval, and block a president from re-declaring the same emergency after Congress rejects it [S3].

Speed up court enforcement of congressional subpoenas, let courts penalize agency heads who knowingly refuse to comply out of their own pockets, and require privilege logs for withheld documents [S3].
Suspend the criminal statute of limitations while a person serves as president or vice president, so no official can run out the clock on federal offenses [S3].

Strengthen whistleblower protections, require cause for removing inspectors general, mandate publication of Justice Department Office of Legal Counsel opinions on budget and spending law, and tighten Hatch Act enforcement against political appointees [S2].
Require federal campaigns to report contacts with foreign nationals and confirm that foreign donations of money or of damaging information about a candidate are illegal [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The sitting president and future presidents, who would lose self-pardon power, unreported emergency powers, and the ability to profit from their businesses while in office; agency heads and political appointees facing personal penalties; and campaigns, which would take on foreign-contact reporting and compliance work.

drawbacks.text: The statute-of-limitations suspension is retroactive and applies to offenses committed before taking office [S3], so a future administration could pursue long-old accusations against a former president years after the fact — an honest supporter must weigh that against the goal of no one being above the law.

Requiring Congress to approve every national emergency within 20 days [S3] could slow or block fast-moving crisis responses if Congress is divided or out of session, trading executive speed for legislative control.
The bill imposes real compliance burdens on political campaigns, which must build foreign-contact reporting systems and risk criminal penalties for reporting lapses [S2].

The expedited subpoena-enforcement and three-judge court procedures [S3] would push more inter-branch disputes into the courts quickly, which courts and civil-liberties groups might resist as straining judicial processes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core purpose — binding, enforceable limits on presidential self-dealing and abuse of power — is served by provisions whose costs are mostly borne by officeholders and campaigns, not the public. The strongest good-faith objections concern the retroactive tolling of statutes of limitations and the speed limits placed on emergency powers, both of which are genuine trade-offs rather than hidden giveaways; on balance the bill's design is coherent, though its breadth invites litigation over nearly every title.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended with no vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill with nine other Democratic senators on September 30, 2021 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day; that referral was the last action ever recorded on the bill [S5].
No committee vote, no Senate floor action, and no roll-call vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Whoever would have been constrained by the bill — sitting and future presidents, political appointees, and officials profiting through private business interests while in office — is better off because it never became law. Nothing in the statute books changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officeholders who would have faced the new limits

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Protecting Our Democracy Act with nine Senate Democratic colleagues.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 30, 2021 and never reported the bill, held no markup, and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans (50 of 50 held every seat needed to block a floor vote)
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; with none supporting it, it had no path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; the visible support was entirely Democratic and Independent — 10 Democratic cosponsors plus 1 Independent, with zero Republican cosponsors [S4].

industries.industry: Business interests tied to the president and senior officials
industries.note: The emoluments title makes it unlawful to accept payments or gifts from foreign or state governments through an official's private business, and lets courts order the money returned [S3]. These businesses profit by trading on official position, which is the direct cost to the public the bill targets.

industries.industry: Foreign governments seeking influence over U.S. officials and campaigns
industries.note: The bill criminalizes foreign gifts to officials and requires campaigns to report foreign contacts, closing channels of foreign influence [S2]. Their loss is the public's gain in election integrity.

Campaigns face new reporting and compliance duties for foreign contacts, with criminal penalties attached [S2]. The burden is real but the protected interest is the integrity of elections in which the public votes.
